lesson.subtitle: Lesson 9 -- What They Said
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Luiz Fernando da Silva | Lesson 9 -- What They Said

listenings.text: The first thing you learn in a newsroom is that there is a difference between what somebody said and what you understood, and that the gap is where almost every complaint comes from. So we have a rule. If you are going to report what a person told you, you have to be able to say which of three things it is. Did they state it as a fact. Did they claim it, which means they said it and we have not checked. Or did they imply it, which means they never said it at all and you have decided what they meant. Those three go in three different sentences, and mixing them up is not a style problem. It is the whole job. And there is a fourth category that people forget. Off the record does not mean secret and it does not mean unusable. It means you may know it, and you may not attribute it. If somebody tells you something off the record and you pass it along with their name on it, you will not get a second conversation with that person, or with anybody they talk to.

I spend a large part of my week reporting conversations upwards, and the mistake I made for the first five years was reporting the mood instead of the words. I would come back from a call and tell my manager that the customer was positive, or that he sounded worried, and none of that survives contact with a decision. What she needed was different. She needed to know that he said he would pay after the second harvest, that he denied having taken product from another supplier, and that he asked whether we would extend the deadline. Three sentences, three verbs, no adjectives. The second thing I learned is to keep what he said separate from what I think he meant. He insisted the delay was the weather. I think he is short of cash. Both of those are useful, and if I put them in the same sentence, my manager cannot tell which one is his and which one is mine.
